newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil Central Bank document takes forward look.
newsitem.headline: Brazil Central Bank document takes forward look.

text.p: A Brazilian Central Bank study is garnering public attention for its dramatic trade liberalization stance and its forward look at the Brazilian economy. The document comes at a time when the government's current reform drive is losing momentum, economists say.
Its author, international affairs director Gustavo Franco, is a leading thinker behind Brazil's successful 2-year-old anti-inflation drive known as the Real Plan.
Franco, a Harvard trained economist, has written dozens of academic papers on the merits of economic stabilization.
"But this paper is important because he wants to take a long-term view of the Real plan and move beyond stabilization," said Alvaro Manoel, director of research at Chase Manhattan bank in Brazil.
Franco, who occupies the No. 2 post at the Central Bank, entitled his 45-page document "Economic Opening and Development".

Economists said Franco's not-so-original prescription is simple: tear down trade barriers, force Brazilian companies to become more productive through greater competition and achieve stable economic growth.
The country's new economic growth model must include wide trade liberalization, "maybe two or three times more than what we have today," Franco writes.

Although Brazil has removed a host of trade barriers over the past few years, it remains a relatively closed economy. Total trade represents just 15 percent of Brazil's gross domestic product, compared to 60 percent in Mexico and 30 percent in Latin America as a whole.
Despite its simplicity, Franco's forward-looking focus could not come at a better time for President Fernando Henrique Cardoso.
Cardoso's constitutional reforms, seen as key to the ultimate success of the Real Plan, are stalled in Congress.

Cardoso reportedly liked the paper so much he made it public. Aides say the president hopes to revive some discussion of Brazil's economic reform drive, a subject that has taken second stage recently to nationwide municipal elections and debate surrounding presidential re-election.
Analysts noted that Franco's treatment of unemployment as a necessary, but temporary, consequence of stabilization undoubtedly pleased the president, who has his eye on re-election in 1998.

"High unemployment has been a big worry for Cardoso. Franco gives him a light at the end of the tunnel by saying continue with privatizations, speed economic opening and at first you will have unemployment but it won't be permanent," said Marcelo Allain, chief economist for BMC bank in Brazil.
It also moves beyond the government's central concern over taming inflation, Allain added.
"It answers the basic question: Now that we have low inflation, what are we going to do? And his answer is economic growth through openness," Allain said.
The document is now making its way through research departments of Brazilian investment banks, where analysts are looking for hints about any upcoming changes to Brazil's stable exchange rate policy.

Franco, who is most closely identified with Brazil's exchange rate policy, has been criticized at home and abroad for maintaining a strong real in the face of large trade deficits and stagnant to modest economic growth.
But based on his latest paper, economists say they do not expect any change in the system, which now allows the real to depreciate by about eight percent a year.
"He doesn't want to use exchange rate policy to tackle trade deterioration and boost growth. This message is very clear," said Marcelo Carvalho, chief economist at JP Morgan in Brazil.

The release of the paper by Cardoso's office has also stirred speculation over future leadership of the Central Bank. A rumor circulated earlier this week that Central Bank President Gustavo Loyola would soon be out. For the first time Franco's name cropped up as the leading contender for the post.
--Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511 232-4411
